title: Telling what already happened
goal: Open the biggest door left: **the past tense**. English often adds -ed; Portuguese changes the verb ending itself — and it does so for every person.
bekal: putting regular -ar, -er, -ir verbs into the past tense
telling about yesterday and last weekend
spotting two small spelling changes in the "I" form

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Como foi o fim de semana?
dialogs.intro: Monday morning. The same question is asked millions of times all over Brazil.

notes: **Every person gets its own past ending.** English changes "work" to "worked" and stops there: I worked, she worked, we worked. Portuguese changes **the verb itself, differently for each person**: *trabalho* becomes *trabalhei*, *trabalha* becomes *trabalhou*. A time word like *ontem* is optional — the verb form already tells you when.
**E aí?** is the most casual Brazilian greeting. Literally "and there?", it means "hey, what's up". Friends use it all day long, often combined: *E aí, tudo bem?*

**Nadamos, comemos, dormimos — notice that the *nós* form is exactly the same as in the present.** *Nós comemos* can mean "we eat" or "we ate", and context decides. That's good news: one less form to memorize.

**Choveu** — weather verbs have only one form, because there's no one doing the action. *Chove* (it rains), *choveu* (it rained), *vai chover* (it's going to rain). Portuguese doesn't even need the empty "it" that English uses.
**Fiquei em casa** — from *ficar*, the all-purpose verb from unit 8. In the past it means "I stayed", "I became", or even "I ended up". *Fiquei feliz* = "I was happy" (I became happy).

grammars.title: The past tense: three groups
body: Drop the infinitive ending and add the endings below. Notice that the stress **moves to the ending** — that's what sounds most different.
after: **Pronunciation to watch:** *falei* = fah-LEY, *falou* = fah-LOH, *comi* = koh-MEE, *comeu* = koh-MAYW, *abriu* = ah-BREEW. All are stressed on **the last syllable** — the opposite of the present, which is stressed on the second-to-last. This stress difference is what your ear will pick up fastest: FAH-loo (I speak) versus fah-LEY (I spoke).
**The -er and -ir groups meet in several rows.** The *eu* form (*comi*, *abri*) and the *nós* form (*comemos*, *abrimos*) follow the same pattern. As usual, you're not memorizing three full systems.

⚠️ **The nós form is the same as in the present** — for all three groups: *nós falamos*, *nós comemos*, *nós abrimos* each cover two tenses at once. So the whole *nós* row needs no new memorizing at all.

grammars.title: Two spelling changes in the "I" form
body: The verb's sound has to stay the same, so the spelling adjusts. There are just three groups, and they only affect the *eu* form.

head: Infinitive
eu (past)
Why
rows: so g stays hard, as in "go"

after: The key: **the sound doesn't change at all** — only the spelling. *Cheguei* is pronounced sheh-GEY, *fiquei* fee-KEY, *dancei* dahn-SEY. If you read them aloud, you'll never go wrong; only your writing hand needs to be careful.
The other rows (você, nós, eles) aren't affected at all: *chegou*, *chegamos*, *chegaram* — all fully regular.

grammars.title: Past time expressions
body: Optional — the verb form already marks the time. But they make your story much clearer.
after: **Passado means "past, last"** and goes after the noun: *semana passada*, *mês passado*, *ano passado*. Compare it with *que vem* for the future from unit 11 — a neat pair.
*Há dois dias* uses the verb *haver* and means "two days ago". In casual conversation Brazilians often swap it for *faz*: *faz dois dias*.

blocks.text: Ten sentences that cover the most common answers to *Como foi o fim de semana?*

head: Português
English
rows: I had lunch with my family.
I met up with some friends.

blocks.text: ⚠️ *Foi* is the past form of both *ser* and *ir* — irregular verbs waiting for you in unit 16. For now memorize *Foi ótimo* and *Foi tranquilo* as whole answers; they'll rescue many a Monday-morning conversation.

**Tranquilo** — pronounced trahn-KWEE-loo — is one of the most Brazilian words there is. It means "calm, relaxed, no problem", and it works as an answer to almost anything. The stretched form, *tranquilão*, is even more laid-back.
Weather verbs have no subject, so they have only one form.
To ask: *Como está o tempo?* ("What's the weather like?"). ⚠️ *O tempo* means "weather" **and** "time" — two quite different meanings, but context always keeps them apart.
